temas.titulo: Book Unit 1 (pp. 6–9, 20) · Clinging to the edge: suspense and verbs
resumen: **Suspense** is a feeling of being **anxious or uncertain about what is about to happen next**. Writers use it as a **device for creating tension**.

Writers often **don't show everything**: *It lurked in the shadows… no human had ever set eyes on its terrifying features…* We never see the creature, so our **imagination** fills the gap – and that is scarier.
## The extract: *The Lastling* by Philip Gross
- **Paris** is on an expedition to the **Himalayas** to find the legendary **yeti** (the *yeh-teh*). She is helped by her friend **Tahr** and by **Geng-sun**, the creature she was hunting.
- She must climb a **rope ladder** and trust the yeh-teh **with her life**. Tahr **loops** a spare rope around her and ties extra knots.
- She is terrified: she nearly **blacks out**, **clamps** herself to the ladder, **hugs** it, her **calf muscles ache and tremble**, she **freezes** and **clings**.

Every sentence has at least one **verb** (a state, an action or a feeling – a 'doing' word). Precise verbs show **exactly** how a character feels or moves: *tremble* shows fear of falling. **froze** is stronger than *stopped*, **clung** than *held*, **looped** than *tied*.
**hissing** = onomatopoeia · **snaked** = metaphor (the rope moves like a snake). **taut** is an **adjective** (tightly stretched) – stronger than *stretched*.

texto.titulo: Clinging to the edge (from The Lastling)
texto.intro: Paris is on an expedition to the Himalayas to find the legendary yeti. She is helped by her friend Tahr and by Geng-sun, the creature she was hunting. *This is a retelling of the extract – read the full text in your English book, page 8. Line numbers match the book.*
parrafos: **Lines 1–6.** The yeh-teh climbs up first. The rope ladder goes **taut**, there is a little **hissing** in the air and the spare rope **snaked** back down. Tahr catches it and tugs it. He explains they will tie it round Paris so the yeh-teh can hold her if… – and then he stops. He doesn't say the word *fall*: it might be too much for her.

**Lines 7–10.** All she has to do is trust the yeh-teh – with her life. Tahr has **looped** the rope around her more than once and tied three or four extra knots, just in case. Then he tells her gently to climb.
**Lines 11–13.** Paris will only climb if Tahr climbs too and keeps talking to her. He asks what about. 'Anything,' she begs – she just needs to know he is there.

**Lines 14–21.** Twice she nearly **blacks out** – and part of her almost wishes she could. She finds herself **clamped** to the ladder, arms through the rungs, **hugging** it with all her strength, eyes shut. She feels safe as long as she never moves again. But her **calf muscles** start to **ache** and tremble, and when she tries to shift her weight the ladder swings away, so she **froze** and **clung** again.
texto.fuente: Retold from *The Lastling* by Philip Gross

temas.titulo: Book Unit 1 (pp. 10–11, 14–15) · Simple, compound and complex sentences
resumen: A **sentence** is a group of words with a **subject**, a **verb** and sometimes an **object** that makes complete sense on its own. It begins with a **capital letter** and ends with a **full stop** (or ? !).
- **Simple**: one **main (independent) clause** – *The teenager was really scared of theme parks.* Use it to state one idea clearly, make important points or ask questions.
- **Compound**: two or more **main clauses** joined by a **conjunction** (and, as, but, because, or, so) – *I am going to the cinema **but** I don't want to see a scary film.*
- **Complex**: one **main clause** + one or more **subordinate (dependent) clauses** – *When it was younger, the ogre was afraid of humans.*
A main clause makes sense on its own; a **subordinate clause must be attached to a main clause**. If the subordinate clause comes first, put a **comma** after it.

They join the subordinate clause to the main clause and always go at the **start of the subordinate clause**: after, although, as, because, before, even though, if, since, unless, until, when, whenever, whereas, wherever, while.

temas.titulo: Book Unit 1 (pp. 12–13) · How will the world end? Satire and adverbs
resumen: **Lord Kelvin** was a **prominent 19th-century scientist**. He predicted that the world's **oxygen** would be used up in about **300 years**. The extract was **published in 1900 by Herbert C. Fyfe**, who describes the views of **Professor Rees** (a prominent American scientist) and Lord Kelvin.
- 'Free as the air we breathe' will become out of date: **air will be manufactured and sold**.
- People who can't work for it or afford it will **perish**.
- Air will be stored in **enormous reservoirs** and **doled out** to families; people will **inhale** it like a **diver**.
- 'Died from **air starvation**' will be common in **coroners' courts**: '**no money, no air**'.
- The wealthy will give **free gifts of air** to the poor at **Christmas**; everyone will wear a great **air helmet**.
- **Silver lining**: Kelvin hopes **agriculturalists** (farmers) will improve plant life so plants absorb the extra **carbonic acid gas** and release oxygen.
A text that uses **humour and exaggeration** to make fun of an idea or a problem. Gifts of air at Christmas and air helmets are exaggerated, comic images.
**Adverbs** give information about **verbs or adjectives** and answer questions like *How?* Many end in **-ly**: *We breathed the air in too **quickly**.*

texto.intro: Lord Kelvin was a prominent 19th-century scientist who made some lively predictions for the future. One of these was that the world's supply of oxygen would be used up in about 300 years. Read the extract published in 1900 by Herbert C. Fyfe as he considers the views of Professor Rees, and Lord Kelvin, describing how the world might end.
parrafos: Professor Rees, a **prominent** American scientist, has been **going further into** the question of the exhaustion of the air supply of the world. He gives definite warning of the coming 'failure' of the air.

"Free as the air we breathe," he writes, will, in the distant future, become an out-of-date, misleading expression. Air will no longer be free, for it will be manufactured and sold like any other **necessary**. Those who will not work for their daily air supply, and who cannot afford to buy it, will **perish**, for Nature will have exhausted her supply. The artificial air will be stored up in enormous reservoirs, and to these receptacles applicants will come for their daily supply of oxygen. This will then be carried home and **doled out** to the family as part of the day's means to support life. The manufactured oxygen will be breathed in as a diver **inhales** the air supplied him when he sinks beneath the waves.

"Died from air starvation" will be a common verdict in the **coroners' courts** of the future, for "no money, no air" will be the rule of life. The wealthy will gain a reputation for charity by free gifts of air to the aged poor at Christmas time. Men and women will no longer be able to look at each other with eyes of love, for everyone will be **clothed** in a great air helmet, like a diver of today.

There is, however, a **silver lining** of hope **fringing** these gloomy clouds of speculation. Lord Kelvin himself is not wholly a prophet of evil, neither are his views of an entirely pessimistic nature. He looks to the **agriculturalist** to improve his methods, so that plant life on the globe may be able to absorb the surplus **carbonic acid gas** and to release sufficient oxygen to cope with the growing consumption of fuel.
glosario: **carbonic acid gas** = heavy gas with no smell, harmful to breathe in
**coroner's court** = court that finds out how a person died
**doled out** = given out in equal shares
**silver lining** = hopeful side of a difficult situation

temas.titulo: Book Unit 1 (pp. 16–19, 21) · Writing suspense: ellipsis, hyphens and planning
resumen: An award-winning author from **Barbados** (a **Caribbean island**; its people are **Bajans/Barbadians**) explains the most important features of writing suspense. His book *Sugar-cane Frame* by **Benjamin Simon** is set in the **sugar-cane industry**.

An **ellipsis** is a series of **three dots** that shows an **omission** (something left out). It can **create suspense**: *I stood at the doorway to the strange old house… I don't remember entering…*

**Hyphens** join two or more words with a **combined meaning**: compound nouns, adjectives or verbs (*fire-fighter, part-time, test-drive*). Some words are hyphenated only to **avoid ambiguity**: *a little-used car*. *re-signed* (signed again) ≠ *resigned* (left the job).
Opening paragraphs must be **fast-paced and eventful** and leave the reader wanting more.
- **Introduction plan**: familiar location, main character (name, gender, age, personality), first or third person, major **crisis**, **dilemma**, **time pressure**.
- **Opening paragraph**: main character, location, crisis, time pressure.
- **Second paragraph**: the dilemma, more details, and a **cliff-hanger**.

temas.titulo: Unseen text 1 · The Light Goes Out
resumen: Practice reading text written for revision: **The Light Goes Out**.
Read the text, then answer the questions in order. Use **short quotations** as evidence.

texto.intro: Mara lives with her father on a tiny island. He is the keeper of the lighthouse.
parrafos: **[1]** The storm arrived just after supper. Wind hurled itself against the lighthouse, and rain rattled the windows like handfuls of gravel. Mara's father pulled on his heavy coat. "I'm going to check the boat," he said. "Stay inside. Whatever happens, keep the lamp burning."

**[8]** "Where did you get that?" Amara whispered.
**[9]** "It was in Great-Aunt Rose's jewellery box," he said. "With a note."
**[10]** "What did the note say?"
**[11]** Kofi's smile faded. He slowly unfolded a yellowed scrap of paper and held it up. Three words were scrawled across it in shaky red ink: *DON'T OPEN IT.*

resumen: Horror and suspense writers use a **toolbox of techniques** to build **tension** and make the reader feel scared or uneasy.
- Typical settings: an abandoned house, a graveyard, a dark forest, a cellar, an empty corridor.
- **Pathetic fallacy**: the weather reflects the mood (a storm, thick fog, a howling wind).
- **Darkness, silence** and **isolation** (a character alone, far from help).
- **Short sentences** to create tension: *Silence. Then a creak.*
- **Simile**: *as cold as ice*, *like a ghost*; **metaphor**: *The corridor was a long, dark throat.*
- **The five senses** to describe what the character sees, hears, smells, touches and tastes.
Opening (normal life / setting) → build-up (something strange) → **climax** (the scariest moment) → resolution or **cliffhanger** (the story ends at a tense moment, without an answer).

resumen: - **Read the extract twice**: once for the story, once looking for details.
- **Retrieve**: find information that is stated directly (who, where, when).
- **Infer**: work out what is **not** said directly, using clues – what a character does, says, looks like and how they react.
- **Use evidence**: back up your answer with a **quotation** from the text.
Writers **show, not tell**: instead of *She was scared*, they write *Her hands trembled and her heart hammered in her chest.*
Clues: **actions** (froze, crept, ran), **body language** (trembling, sweating, wide eyes), **speech** (whispered, stammered, screamed), **thoughts**.

temas.titulo: Setting and writing with the five senses
resumen: The **setting** is **where** and **when** a story takes place, and the **atmosphere** (mood) of that place.
- **Place**: a haunted mansion, a forest, a cellar.
- **Time**: midnight, a winter evening, long ago.
- **Weather and light**: fog, storms, flickering candles, moonlight.
- 👃 **smell** – *the air stank of damp and decay*
- ✋ **touch / feel** – *the icy handle stung her fingers*
- 👅 **taste** – *the metallic taste of fear filled his mouth*
Using the senses puts the reader **inside** the scene.

resumen: - **Proper nouns**: names of particular people, places, days, months – always a **capital letter**: *Sofia, London, Monday, October*.
- **Abstract nouns**: things you can't see or touch – feelings and ideas: *fear, terror, courage, silence, darkness*.
- **Collective nouns**: a group – *a flock of birds, a swarm of bees, a pack of wolves*.
Adjectives describe nouns: *the **old**, **creaking** door*. Choose **precise** adjectives: *big* → *enormous, gigantic*; *scary* → *terrifying, sinister*.
- An **expanded noun phrase** adds detail to a noun: *the crumbling house on the hill*.
- Use commas between two or more adjectives: *a dark, narrow corridor*.
- Comparatives and superlatives: *dark → darker → darkest*; *terrifying → more terrifying → most terrifying*.

resumen: A **clause** is a group of words with a **subject** and a **verb**. A **main clause** makes sense on its own.
- **Compound**: two main clauses joined by a **co-ordinating conjunction** (**FANBOYS**: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) – *The door creaked **and** the candle went out.*
- **Complex (multi-clause)**: a main clause + a **subordinate clause** – *The candle went out **when** the door creaked.*
## Subordinating conjunctions – I SAW A WABUB!
- A subordinating conjunction is the **first word** of a subordinate clause.
- A **subordinate clause** does **not make sense on its own**, but always has a subject and a verb (*after she smiled* ✓; *after Christmas* ✗ – no verb, so 'after' is a preposition).
- If the subordinate clause comes **first**, put a **comma** after it: ***When the bell rang**, the pupils sped into school.*

resumen: - **Capital letters**: start of a sentence, names (proper nouns), 'I'.
- **Full stop** . at the end of a statement · **question mark** ? · **exclamation mark** ! for shock or surprise.
- **Commas**: in lists, after a subordinate clause at the start, between adjectives.
- **Apostrophes**: **contraction** (missing letters: *don't = do not*, *it's = it is*) and **possession** (belonging: *the ghost's chain*; plural *the ghosts' chains*).
- **Speech marks** "…": around the words spoken; new speaker = new line; punctuation goes **inside**: *"Who's there?" she whispered.*
Keep the same **tense** (stories are usually in the **past tense**). Paragraph when the **time, place, topic or speaker** changes (**TiPToP**).
